content.thinking:
I'm setting up a root joint plus a hinge for the chest lid, and planning the overall design: a League of Legends-style exaggerated, high-contrast hoard scene with an ornate chest, mounded coins, and glowing gem crystals.

I'm sizing the whole prop group around 1.6m, with the chest roughly 0.9m wide by 0.55m deep by 0.6m tall, surrounded by a coin mound. I'm planning the top-down composition to include an octagonal stone dais with a glowing cyan rune ring and gold trim, using a palette of gold, teal-cyan magic, purple gems, and crimson velvet against dark navy stone.

Now I'm positioning the chest toward the back-left of the dais with a slight rotation, and starting to define its body shape.

Designing chest body details...

Working out the lid geometry, deciding to extrude an arched semicircle profile along the thickness axis, then figuring out the hinge joint and open rotation angle so the lid tilts back dramatically to reveal glowing coin piles inside.

With the lid opened 70°, it rises roughly half a meter, giving a total height around a meter plus whatever crowns the pile. For the coin heaps, I'll merge geometry per color into mounds of 400+ low-poly cylinders using a few gold and silver tones to keep the part count manageable.

I'm figuring the triangle budget stays under control with 8-sided coins, but texturing can't apply to merged parts, so I'm planning a handful of standout hero coins with decal textures, plus painted coin stacks using gold stripe patterns, and an overall mound shape built from a lathed profile with a mottled gold coin-scale texture.

Rather than scattering individual coins on the mound surface with ray-casting, I'm considering building a custom heightfield mesh from summed gaussian bumps as a single cohesive hoard shape, painted directly using position and normal data since there's no UV mapping needed.

Switching to a polar grid for the heap—rings and segments producing a few hundred triangles with flat faceted shading for a low-poly look. I'm computing the height as a sum of bumps multiplied by a falloff that smooths to zero at the radius edge, sitting on top of a dais floor, with the chest embedded into the back of the heap.

For the chest placement, it sits at the back with the opening facing forward toward the camera, partially buried by heap lumps piling around its front and sides. I'm planning to scatter around 350 coins across the heap surface, tilted randomly based on surface normals, using a mix of gold, pale gold, amber, and silver tones for contrast.

For the chest's interior, I want a domed pile of coins rising slightly above the rim, treated as part of the same heightfield so it reads naturally through the open lid while the solid chest walls hide the sides of that interior pile.

Now I'm planning the gem shapes—stretched octahedrons for rubies, prismatic clusters with pointed tips for cyan crystals, bevel-edged boxes for emerald cuts, and lathe-based crown/pavilion profiles for round brilliant cuts—with glow effects applied.

Picking a distinct glowing color per gem type (ruby, sapphire, cyan, emerald, amethyst, topaz) while staying mindful of the color limit, and giving each glow its own material. I'm also designing a hero crown resting tilted on the heap, with an exaggerated League-style band, five tall spikes tipped with gems, a glowing blue center gem, and a crimson velvet interior, sized around 0.2m diameter and 0.15m tall.

Settling on a slightly larger 0.24m diameter so the crown reads clearly as a chunky, stylized object within the 2m scene. Working out how to construct it in local coordinates and then place it correctly using a transform matrix, considering helper functions to position vertices before merging the lathe and extrude geometries into the final mesh.

For the goblets, I'm planning three: one standing upright on the dais, jeweled and gold with a ruby band and glowing cyan or wine-red liquid, one tipped over spilling coins, and one resting on the heap. Each built from a lathed profile with foot, knotted stem, and bowl, gold-painted with gem studs around the rim and a glowing liquid disc inside, sized around 0.22m tall for realism.

I'm also thinking about additional hoard pieces beyond coins, gems, chest, crown, and goblets—a pearl necklace draped as a sweep of spheres, a burlap sack tipped over spilling coins, a golden ring with a gem, a chain necklace with a large pendant, and a stack of trapezoid gold ingots on the right for silhouette interest. I might also add a few hovering magic motes or glowing gems for extra atmosphere.

For sparkle effects, I'll keep floating sparkles low and close to the heap to avoid inflating the model's bounding box, using small cross or four-point star sparkle cards in cyan/white with glow rather than light beams (which won't work well given alpha-test-only materials). I'll also add a glowing rune ring on the dais for extra detail, then shift focus to making sure the design reads clearly from a top-down view.

For the dais itself, I'm defining it as a round lathe shape with a radius of 1.5 and thickness 0.08, using a dark slate-blue stone base with gold inlay and a glowing cyan rune ring near the rim, visible around the central heap. The rune ring will be a flat circle texture with transparency, placed just above the dais surface, drawn with stroke outlines, tick marks, and hex rune symbols.

I'm building the dais from layered lathe shapes -- a wide stone base, a thin gold trim ring, and a top disc -- with the paint function coloring tiles based on radial distance from center so the gold ring and flagstone cells appear procedurally.

Now I'm designing the chest: a mahogany-red wooden body with vertical plank grain texture, gold trim bands across the front, chunky corner pieces, a big lock plate with a glowing cyan hextech gem, arched lid with gold banding, rivets made from merged spheres, gold ring handles on the sides, and a crimson velvet lining inside the lid.

I'm working out the chest proportions and lid geometry: width 0.95, depth 0.6, body height 0.42, lid arch rising 0.18 above the body, opened at roughly 100° so it leans slightly past vertical. I'm figuring out how to build the lid as a solid extruded arch shape so the underside shows the velvet lining when open, rather than a hollow shell.

I'm identifying that the extrude's bottom face, where the normal points downward, gets painted with crimson velvet and a gold quilted pattern, while the rest of the surface gets the exterior trim.

Now I'm planning the gold bands across the lid as separate thin extrudes offset slightly from the main arch outline, with coordinate axes mapped so local x becomes world z, and setting up the chest's depth orientation with the back and front faces positioned along that axis.

Still working out the arch geometry...

Now I'm setting up the lid's hinge joint, positioning it along the top back edge of the chest and defining its rotation axis so it swings open to about 100 degrees, leaning back as a backdrop behind the chest while the interior contents remain tucked underneath.

Writing placement helper logic...

Now I'm moving into the actual scene coordinates, starting with the dais top height set at 0.08 and working outward from there.

For the coin heap, I want a heightfield centered on the dais, with the chest footprint occupying the interior and gaussian bumps building up the surrounding mound. I'm sketching out the chest's dimensions (feet height, body height) to figure out where the heap needs to reach F+0.54, and deciding that rather than forcing a smooth gaussian to match that flat interior height, I should build the gem/coin fill inside the chest as its own dedicated geometry rather than relying purely on the heightfield.

I'm picturing a squashed low-poly sphere scaled to a dome shape, painted with a faceted coin pattern, hidden partially by the chest rim, which handles the chest-interior fill cleanly. Outside the chest I'll place a few gaussian bumps for the spilled coin piles -- one in front where coins cascade out from the lip, and two more to either side -- each with its own position, height, and spread to vary the mound's silhouette.

I'm adding more flank and scatter bumps behind and around the chest to widen the heap naturally, using a falloff function based on distance from center so the pile tapers smoothly at the edges without z-fighting against the dais floor. Now I'm thinking through where to place the goblets and crown on top of these piles -- the crown tilted on the left mound, one goblet standing upright and stable on a flat dais spot, another tipped over and spilling coins on the right pile, and a third goblet upright elsewhere on the heap.

I'm reconsidering putting the crown front-and-center on the pile's peak for a classic "crown atop treasure" look, but realizing that position would bury the chest's lock plate under the pile height -- so I'm adjusting the spill's height and spread so the lock plate stays visible while the crown still sits prominently near the peak.

Repositioning the crown to the left pile keeps the lock plate visible, and I'll put a ruby cluster plus larger gems in the central spill area.

Settling on three goblets: one tall upright on the left dais, one tipped over spilling coins and gems nearby, and a squat jeweled chalice near the crown pile on the right. I'm also placing a slumped sack spilling coins at the back-left, with an ingot stack balancing the right side.

For jewels, I'm adding glowing hexagonal crystal clusters flanking the chest at both back corners — mostly cyan with a magenta accent, varying heights up to 0.7m for a magical League-style silhouette. I'll scatter around 25 cut gems across the heap with a large ruby prominent on the front pile, keeping the overall scene diameter around 3 units.

Checking the scale, I want to settle dais radius at 1.4 and heap radius at 1.2, verifying the gem and crystal positions all stay within that bound. The tallest element — the open chest lid plus crystals — comes out to roughly 1.2m total height, which feels right for the proportions.

Now I'm picking a color palette: warm golds and bronzes for metal trim, a reddish-brown wood with deep crimson velvet accents, cool slate-blue stones, and a glowing cyan for the magic effects.

I'm also adding a set of gem colors (magenta, ruby, emerald, amethyst, sapphire, topaz), silver tones, and burlap/rope textures, keeping the total palette under 64 colors. I'm leaning toward painterly shading with manual gradient highlights rather than flat cel-shading, matching League's style of high-contrast but softly lit rendering.

I'm defining a gold paint function that mixes dark and light gold based on surface normal direction (brighter on upward-facing surfaces) plus noise for a hand-painted streaky look, then planning a similar cell-based pattern for coin textures.

Blending in a warm highlight tint based on surface normal brightness. I'm also estimating texel density across the heap and dais surfaces to pick a paint resolution—2048 seems like a reasonable balance against atlas size limits.

Now I'm planning out roughly 400 parts organized into merged buckets for variety, and setting up the builder infrastructure with imports for geometry merging utilities. I'm defining the root joint at the origin and starting to attach child joints like the chest lid, hinged off the base.

Setting up bucket and matrix helper functions...

Now I'm designing coin geometry as small cylinders placed along the heap surface, orienting each one's normal using finite-difference sampling of the height field.

I'm figuring out the coin count budget: around 420 for the main heap, plus chest fill, scattered loose coins, and a few standing on edge rolling, each using roughly 32 triangles so the total stays around 17-18k triangles. I'm also considering adding a bit of color variation and a subtle emblem detail to a few "hero coins" to break up the repetition.

For texturing standing/leaning coins, I'm thinking about whether a cylinder's UV mapping would stretch an engraved crest decal unpleasantly across the thin side versus just applying the texture cleanly to the circular cap, possibly using a separate decal circle slightly offset from the coin face with a transparent background so the engraving reads clearly without distortion.

Then I realize this approach could scale: since all the circular decals can share one texture, I can merge them into a single batched part using matrices for placement, just like the untextured geometry merging. That means potentially decorating hundreds of coins with an emblem decal for only a modest triangle cost, so I'll apply this to the top-facing coins that need the engraved look.

For the decal artwork, I'm sketching a small coin emblem — a dark amber outer ring, a lighter inner ring, and a central diamond/gem shape with facet highlights — rendered on a transparent background so the coin's own color shows through underneath. Since coins come in varied golds and a few silvers, I need the decal coloring to still read well when placed on either base color.

For arrangement, I'm planning to build coin stacks out of individual cylinder coins stacked with slight random offsets and rotations for a natural, wobbly pile look, with decals applied to the top coin, then placing several of these stacks within the scene.

For the gems, I'm building faceted shapes using combined cylinder and cone geometries to fake a lathe-cut brilliant cut gem, with a flat-shaded crown and pointed pavilion, and grouping gems by color so glow effects can apply to merged geometry per color bucket.

But I'm realizing full-strength glow risks washing out the faceted shading since emissive color could saturate the surface and hide the facet edges. I'm thinking I should reserve strong glow only for the crystal/magic gem types and keep other gems lower-emissive or unlit so their cut facets stay visible.

A better trick: bake the faceted shading directly into a texture with a gradient (bright core fading to darker edges), mapped so the cylinder's UV wrap creates alternating light/dark columns that read as facets even under full glow. Since CylinderGeometry's UV wraps evenly around the radial segments, I can paint six alternating bright/dark stripes into the texture so glow preserves the faceted look instead of flattening it, and I can apply the same trick to the cone tip using its radial UV wrap.

I need a separate crystalTex function per hue (cyan, magenta, green, etc.) generating an SVG with alternating-lightness columns plus a vertical gradient, using explicit rects rather than relying on linear gradients rasterizing correctly in-browser.

For small cut gems I'll lower glow intensity to around 0.35-0.5 so the emissive tint adds shine without washing out the facet shading, then bucket the gems on the heap by hue.

Now I'm defining the gem geometry builders: brilliant cuts merge a tapered cylinder crown with an inverted cone pavilion tilted and half-sunk into the heap, octahedral shapes stretch an octahedron vertically for rubies, and emerald cuts use a flattened tapered box...

For scattering, I'm placing around 45 gems across the pile with chunky random sizes between 0.03-0.07, plus a few exaggerated hero gems at 0.09 scale -- including a giant stretched ruby octahedron front-center and possibly a floating cyan crystal accent.

Actually I like the idea of a glowing cyan faceted gem hovering inside the open chest, around 0.13 size with soft glow and maybe thin gold orbit rings around it for that magical League-style effect.

Now I'm sketching crystal clusters for the back corners—low-poly hex-shaped crystals built from a cylinder body plus a cone tip, keeping radial segments low so they read as faceted gems rather than smooth shapes.

Each face of the hex prism gets its own uv column so a gradient texture gives distinct shading per facet, with the cone's uv matching the cylinder's so the glow reads consistently top to bottom. I'm sinking the crystal bases into small rock clusters made from flattened, mottled low-poly dodecahedrons for a stony anchor.

For color, I'm leaning into high-contrast saturated accents like LoL style rather than one signature hue—left cluster glowing cyan-teal, right cluster a violet-magenta, each cluster holding 5-6 leaning crystals sized between 0.15 and 0.7 tall.

Now I'm blocking out the chest dimensions: roughly 1.0 wide, 0.62 deep, 0.40 tall body sitting above 0.06-tall feet, with a slightly flared silhouette built from a box plus trim rather than a true frustum.

I'm adding wider molding slabs at the base and top of the chest, then working out how to paint vertical wood-plank grain onto the body—accounting for the chest's slight yaw by converting world points into the chest's local coordinate space before computing plank seams so the lines stay aligned rather than skewing.

Writing plank seam logic...

Still defining grain streak direction, then moving to colors: dark and light wood tones, seam shadows, and a gilded edge highlight on top faces. I'm also planning the chest's corner feet as squat gold ball or frustum shapes to match the chunky stylized look.

Now I'm adding the trim details: gold base and top moldings slightly wider than the chest body, vertical gold bands with rivet rows along the front and sides, and L-shaped corner guard plates wrapping each vertical edge for a reinforced, armored look.

Then I'm designing the front lock plate as a shield-shaped gold extrusion with beveled edges, a glowing cyan keyhole slot, and a ring of small cyan studs around it, plus a connecting lock hasp strap running from lid to body.

For the hasp itself, I'm making the tongue part of the lid so it hangs down over the lock when closed and lifts with the lid when opened. Then I'm adding side iron ring handles on gold mount plates, rivet spheres along the metal bands, and planning a painted filigree swirl decal for the front panels.

Now I'm sizing those decal panels to fit the gaps between the lock plate and the side bands, giving them a gold swirl-and-gem pattern, and adding a matching decal to the lid front. For the interior, I'm thinking through the inner crimson velvet border frame that sits just below the rim, inside the hollow body.

For the top lip, I'm picturing a gold rectangular ring frame right at the rim with the coin fill dome poking through its inner opening, sized so the dome's ellipsoid edges align with the frame's inner edge, leaving a thin crimson velvet reveal in the gap if needed -- though if the dome matches the inner frame exactly, I can skip adding a separate velvet slab underneath.

Now I'm scattering individual coin shapes across the dome's curved surface to give it texture, then moving to the lid: an extruded arch shape with wood planks on the outside and velvet lining the bottom, defined by a flat base rising into a smooth rounded arc using several curve segments to avoid sharp corners.

Setting up the hinge pivot, I offset the lid's outline coordinates so the hinge point becomes the local origin, letting the lid rotate open and closed around that edge naturally. I'm also adding a velvet pad with gold stitching as a decal on the underside of the lid, oriented to face outward and inherit the lid's rotation when it swings open.

Next I'm working on the gold bands that trace the arch of the lid, building them as an offset/padded version of the same outline so they sit slightly outside the lid's surface.

Working out band and hasp placement, then adding rivets as small spheres positioned along each band's outline curve, roughly 25 rivets total across the lid. Now planning the hinge knuckles as gold cylinders along the rear edge.

For the gem and interior, I'm placing a large faceted cabochon at the hasp's center band apex, then considering that since the lid is open, the viewer actually sees the velvet-lined interior with gold stitching and the hasp tongue, while the gem and exterior back face away from camera.

Since the underside is the most visible surface, I want to make it the real showpiece: a rich gold filigree crest emblem on crimson velvet, framed by a diamond lattice quilting pattern with a glowing central gem, covering most of the interior panel with decorative borders.

Now I'm moving on to building the crown mesh — shaping its lathe profile with flared radii from base to top, defining the wall thickness and outline points, and adding a subtle cyan glow trim around the band.

Still designing crown geometry...

Working out the radial geometry for each spike: tangent and radial-outward vectors at angle φ define the extrusion axes, with the spike base slightly embedded in the band and leaning outward since crowns typically taper that way.

I set the extrusion's "up" direction to tilt radially outward by about 7 degrees, confirming it stays orthogonal to the tangent direction, with a thin 0.012 thickness and slight bevel. Now I'm planning the crossed arched bands that sweep over the top toward the center orb, sketching out catmull-rom control points along the arc path.

Each arch sweeps between the rim and an apex point, with a second arch rotated 90° to cross the first at the top. I'm deciding on an apex ornament — settling on a cyan gem octahedron rather than a cross or cone finial — and working out total crown height, landing on roughly 0.27 once spikes, arches, and the apex gem are stacked.

Inside, I'm adding a velvet dome cap visible through the arches, plus a jeweled band circling the base with alternating ruby, diamond, and emerald settings on gold pads, placed using a ring helper around an upward-facing frame.

I'm also planning an engraved zigzag pattern along the band's top and bottom edges, painted dark against gold highlights to give it a lathed, decorative texture.

Now I'm designing the goblet shape as a lathed profile, mapping out the foot disc, stem, knot, bowl, and rim as a sequence of radius/height points so it can be revolved into a closed outline, with a separate inner profile needed to give the bowl a hollow shell.

For the fill, I'm planning differentiated contents per goblet: A gets a glowing cyan elixir with bubbles, B (tipped) has coins streaming from its mouth with no liquid, and C holds a heaped mound of merged gems. I'll also add a ring of six outward-facing gem studs around each bowl plus a gold torus rim.

For material variety I'm mixing metals and gems across the three goblets — gold with ruby, gold with emerald, and a silver variant with sapphire for contrast — and I'm working out the tilt rotation and placement for the tipped goblet B so its mouth faces toward the viewer, planning to test the orientation visually.

Writing lathe handle code...

Now I'm placing a burlap sack near the heap, tilted toward the coin pile with its neck gathered and flared open, coins spilling from the mouth, and planning a woven burlap texture pattern for the paint.

I'll add a rope tie at the neck with a knotted sphere and tail sweeps, plus a stitched patch on the belly using painted weave lines based on surface coordinates rather than actual geometry. Then I'm moving on to designing gold ingots as trapezoidal prisms.

For each ingot, I'll extrude a trapezoid cross-section along its length with a slight bevel, then stamp a small emblem decal on top. I'm arranging six ingots into a pyramid stack (3-2-1) on the dais, finished with a gold paint material.

Rather than placing stamps individually, I'll merge them into one textured part using plane geometries per ingot top, grouped by shared texture identity via a Map, and generalizing a `putTex` helper so colored textures auto-default to white base color. I want to confirm identical plane/circle geometries with matching indexed attributes will merge correctly before moving on to designing the necklace—pearls on a catmull-rom path with a pendant draped around the front of the pile.

For the necklace, I'm sweeping a thin gold chain along a curved path over the heap's front lip down to rest near center, adding pearl spheres along it, and deciding the pendant should simply be the big ruby already placed there to avoid duplicating gemstones. Then for sparkles, I'm considering star-shaped glowing cards (white/cyan) as plane geometry parts, though I need to figure out how to orient them to face the camera.

For placement I'm scattering about 14 of these glowing star cards around the hoard at varying heights (0.15-0.9), keeping them under 1.2m, with small size and crossed-plane geometry for a glint effect. Now I'm working out the dais design using a lathe shape with 16 segments, painting it procedurally based on radius: a dark-blue stone rim, a gold inlay ring, a rune channel with glowing cyan decal, and stone plates filling the inner area.

I'm carving block lines into the paint every 22.5 degrees for texture, then refining the dais's radial profile with a chamfer at the outer bevel where gold trim goes, settling on 24 segments for a smoother round shape. I'm also sorting out how the rune decal (a circle texture 2.6m wide) sits just above the dais surface so the heap of treasure covering the center doesn't completely hide it.

I'm working out precise height offsets to avoid z-fighting between the dais top, the rune decal, and the heap's falloff boundary, settling on the decal sitting 1.5mm above the dais and the heap edge rising another 2.5mm beyond that so the rune band (radius 1.18–1.30m) stays visible outside the heap's footprint. Now I'm mapping those meter measurements into SVG viewBox units to draw the actual rune ring strokes.

I'll settle on dais radius 1.5 (3.0m diameter) with the rune band spanning 1.15–1.40, mapping that to the SVG viewBox scale so the texture covers the full 3.0m prop size.

Objects within radius 1.1 are safe, with the heap's radial falloff spanning 0.85 to 1.1. I'm also planning 24 merged gold bosses spaced around the dais rim as decorative studs.

Thinking through the top-down color scheme (gold heap, dark red chest, cyan accents) and the heap's polar grid geometry -- 16 rings and 32 sectors giving around 1024 triangles, with nonuniform radial spacing via a power curve and flat-shaded normals computed per face.

I'm adding lumpy noise to the heap surface using combined sine waves to simulate uneven coin piles, with finite-difference normals for proper lighting, then scattering coins while excluding areas inside the chest's footprint box so coins don't overlap with it or other props like goblets.

I'm defining a keepOut list of circles to exclude coin placement near object footprints, sampling roughly 520 candidate positions across the heap plus 90 extra coins filling the chest's ellipsoid shape, then layering in 40 scattered gems and setting up a gold-dominant color distribution for the coins.

Checking the triangle budget now: coins, heap, gems, crystals, and the lathed chest/goblet meshes should total around 35k triangles, comfortably under the 60k cap, with coin mesh resolution fine enough to avoid flagging in quality checks.

Now I'm setting up a helper Loc class that stores a position and quaternion derived from Euler angles for placing objects in the scene.

I'm defining a point-tuple type and working out how placed objects like the lathe and extrusions get their position and axis from world-space helpers, plus how painting handles local coordinates for rotated objects like the chest. Now I'm setting up a global height function and starting to write out the detailed implementation code in sections.

Writing imports and setup...

Still writing SVG code...

Checking the vertex alignment: tracing how rotating the circle geometry by -90° about X maps its vertices onto the XZ plane, and comparing phase against the cylinder's octagon vertices to see if they share the same 8-fold symmetry orientation.

For the crystal texture, I'm planning a simple SVG approach: six vertical columns each with a gradient from dark base to bright tip, then overlaying semi-transparent black rectangles with varying opacities per column to simulate alternating facet brightness, keeping everything fully opaque since it's a texture map.

I also need to handle UV mapping separately for the cone tip versus cylinder body so the gradient doesn't restart at the cone's base — remapping the cone's v-coordinate into the upper portion of the texture range so the color continues smoothly from where the cylinder leaves off.

For the rune ring texture on the dais, I'm planning to generate 24 angular glyph shapes arranged radially around the circle, each rotated into its own segment with consistent stroke widths, plus outer and inner band circles and small triangle accents in cyan tones.

Now I'm designing a gold scroll ornament decal for the chest panels using a symmetric vine-and-leaf path with gem circles, scaled appropriately for the panel size, and planning a second variant with gold lines and red dots for dark wood panels.

For the lid's velvet quilting texture, I'm sketching a diamond lattice pattern with a double-line border and a central star emblem featuring a cyan gem, plus small gold circles marking the button crossings. I'm also working through the tricky orientation math for how this underside texture should face once the lid is opened to 100 degrees.

Next I'll design simpler stamp textures: an ingot stamp with a crown-like diamond-and-bars emblem, and a sparkle star texture using layered 4-point star polygons in white and cyan for the glow effect. I'm also planning to draw a lock/keyhole shape directly with geometry rather than a texture—just a glowing disc plus a dark rectangular slot.

For gems, I'll skip facet texturing and rely on smooth lathed shading, which should look fine. For the gold paint function, I'm blending dark and bright gold tones based on surface normal and noise, with a highlight boost near the top-facing areas—normal lighting on top of that should be enough. For the chest body, I'll paint the box with a wood texture using plank lines based on surface position.

Writing wood plank texture function...

Now I'm sketching the chest's local geometry: setting its origin relative to Lc with a slight yaw rotation for visual interest, and starting to define overall dimensions like width and depth before working out foot height.

I'm planning out the body section with a helper function that places each box piece (feet, body, lid) at local coordinates with the correct bone attachment and paint color.

For the base and top moldings, I'm defining them as gold-painted ring frames built from front/back/side box segments, sized slightly larger than the body with inset edges to form a decorative lip.

For the corner posts, I'm placing four vertical boxes at each corner using a darker bronze-gold paint to distinguish them from the main gold trim, giving them a riveted, structural look.

Now I'm adding vertical decorative bands across the front, back, and sides using the darker gold paint, then scattering small highlighted rivet spheres along each band for detail, and setting up a lock plate shape centered on the front face.

Still shaping the lock plate...

Positioning details continuing: side torus handles, corner feet cylinders, and decal panel placement on front and back, sizing the panels to fit between the lock plate and side bands.

Now I'm shaping the lid itself as an arched extrusion, setting its thickness along the width axis with beveled edges and wood paint coloring, bound to a hinge pivot.

I need to figure out where the hinge sits relative to the raised frame -- since the frame rises above the body top, the lid's hinge point has to be positioned higher too, so the lid bottom doesn't collide with the frame geometry when closed.

Making the lid slightly larger than the body footprint to overhang the frame, then figuring out positioning for the decorative bands on the lid, including the end bands near the outer edges.

Shaping the hasp tongue outline hanging from the lid's top lip, pointed at the bottom to overlap the lock plate on the body below.

Good, that overlap makes it read like a hasp engaged with the lock plate. For the lid I still need rivets on the bands, hinge barrels with cylinders at the back mounted along x with their pins, the underside decal, and a glowing ruby cabochon set into the tongue at the lid's front center.

Now I'm working out the pose rotation for opening the lid — rotating about the local x-axis by a negative angle so the front tips upward instead of down, confirming the sign convention holds once yaw is applied, landing on roughly -105° to open it.

Checking the resulting geometry: at that rotation the lid's highest point sits around 1.25m total height, with the back edge of the arched lid swinging backward to about z=-0.9, which overlaps the chest body's rear footprint.

The crystals at ±0.85 stay comfortably within the lid's width. I'm also verifying the velvet underside of the open lid faces outward toward the camera at this angle, which it does nicely, and now working out the dome shape for the hoard fill inside the chest.

I'm shaping a flattened ellipsoid dome scaled to fit the chest interior, scattering gems and coins across its surface, then positioning the crown on the left pile with a slight yaw to angle it toward the viewer.

For the tilt, I'm leaning the crown back and adding roll so its low edge sinks into the heap based on sampled height at the ring's base, with the goblet following the same height-sampling logic—leaving final tuning for visual review. I'll place the sack near the low-height region on the far side too.

For the heap spilling near the sack, I'm adding coin bumps around it and a larger pile to its right. The ingots on the dais get positioned as a small stack with yawed orientation, working out spacing and dimensions for a bottom row of three.

Still arranging ingot rows...

Now I'm planning the crystal clusters as grouped geometries combining a tapered cylinder base with a cone tip, defining each cluster by position, height, radius, and lean offsets.

I'm positioning crystals embedded into the ground with a slight lean, orienting each by composing a transform from Euler rotations, and building a rocky base from a scaled icosahedron with mottled dark coloring, plus scattering a few small rock fragments nearby before placing a floating gem above the chest.

For the floating gem, I'm shaping a faceted crystal using a crown and cone pavilion, giving it a cyan glow at moderate strength so the flat facets stay visible under lighting, then surrounding it with two tilted gold rings and three small orbiting octahedron gems at ring positions.

I'm positioning the gem cluster above the chest near the lid, accepting some overlap with the velvet decal, and setting up sparkle cards to stand upright facing the camera along the z-axis so they read clearly as flat star shapes rather than lying flat.

For extra treasure details, I'm adding small gold rings with gems scattered around the pile, plus scattered white pearl spheres mixed in near the necklace area. I'm also sketching out a goblet-building function that takes metal, gem, and fill parameters so I can vary liquid or gem fills inside the cup shape.

Working out the goblet outline points...
